items.text: – Why didn't you go to the marmal house?
items.q: Ghassem, a boy, repeats his own mistake 'marmal' for marble. Does 'marmal house' read as a child's word, not a typo?
before: …It was red. Like that same big red door. I sat beside the gutter. I put my feet in the gutter. There was no water. It was empty inside my heart. The man came back. The front wheel wasn't turning anymore. He slapped Omid. We both cried. The man left. Ghassem came back. He scolded us. He said:

items.text: – Fine, Eagle Eye, fine. Now don't stick your glasses into the laptop.
items.q: Hooman teases short-sighted Sajad, nicknamed Eagle Eye, who peers very close to his laptop. Does the teasing land?
before: He narrowed his eyes behind his glasses and brought his head close to his laptop screen.
– If you don't believe it, come see for yourself, objectively.

items.text: With trembling hands I flipped frantically through the ghazals, searching for the Hafez beit that, like the painting, as that other girl had said, would make us more shit-dizzy the deeper we sank into it.
items.q: Amir echoes a girl's crude made-up word for baffling. Does 'shit-dizzy' read naturally in his own storytelling?

items.text: The boy has bent down and rubs just below his knee with his hand.
items.q: The boy has run into a low brick wall. Is it clear he is rubbing the spot just below his knee?
Maman, hard of hearing, catches only one word of Ghassem's joke about Baba. Does her short question sound natural?
before: – Then just think what our poor Baba must be going through: sitting idle at home all these years.

items.q: Amir mishears 'peer-to-peer' as Persian pir, meaning elder, which fits his nicknames. Does the mishearing come through?
before: – Some kind of peer-to-peer electronic money.

items.text: – God willing, may you always be araasteh.
items.q: The guard puns on the Persian word araasteh, meaning neat and well-groomed. Does his blessing read naturally?

items.text: – Yes, I wiw buy you a dolly. When I get some money I wiw buy you an even better one, Baba's girl.
items.q: Her father answers, tenderly echoing her baby talk. Does 'wiw' read as playful, not a typo?
before: – Vwoooom! Baba, Baba, wiw you buy me dis big dolly?
A voice comes from behind me:

items.text: – The boys in the room picked the perfect name for you. Sometimes you really do make a mess of things and miss the mark. Of course I mean you, my Tavvy.
items.q: Niloofar teases Amir, shortening his dorm nickname Taverny. Does 'my Tavvy' sound affectionate and natural?
before: – No, of course not, the old man sitting on that other bench.
I looked. An old man had leaned his cane against the bench and was busy reading a newspaper.

items.text: – Can you explain what your relationship with your male relatives is like? Because I've heard that in Tehran ...
items.q: Amir means her boy cousins and the other young men in her family. Is 'male relatives' clear for that?
before: She gave a slight nod. Happy with what I thought was a way forward, I continued.

items.text: – Eldie, see how far you've taken it: Farid, who doesn't give a damn about us or the room or anyone, has spoken up.
items.q: Hooman, the crudest talker in the room, says this. Does 'doesn't give a damn' sound as coarse as he would be?
before: It was the last time Farid responded to anything said or done in the room without someone addressing him directly. Hooman said:

items.text: Laughing, Hooman thumps me hard on the back, and the sugar cube jumps in my throat.
items.q: Amir is holding a sugar cube in his mouth while drinking tea. Is it clear he nearly chokes on it?

items.text: After a while he started posting about the decline of modern man because of social media, and no one was there to tell him, 'You fossil, you're a monument to stupidity and decline,' haha.
items.q: Hooman laughs about an old roommate's online posts. Does his mocking insult sound natural and funny?

items.text: – The hope of union with you keeps me alive; or else my every breath, parted from you, would be the dread of death.
items.q: Amir reads Niloofar a line of Hafez. Does it read as poetry, with a clear meaning?
before: – What share? It's nothing but torment and loneliness. I really don't understand what you've set your heart on. I opened the book and read:

items.text: Poke your head into every nook and cranny. The old folks always said, peek into every last corner.
items.q: Maman quotes an old saying, kept close to the Persian. Is its meaning clear here?
before: – Mm-hm, you're doing the right thing. While you have the chance, go see all the villages.

items.text: – Pfff, damn you. You've become an expatriate now, so you don't give a damn about us. You foreigner-worshiping sellout.
items.q: Hooman, crude and half joking, scolds his old friend for moving abroad. Does this sound like how he would really talk?
before: …part, where it narrows and goes almost to the Valiasr gate, it becomes a hundred seventy meters. Damn you, you dragged me a hundred seventy meters after you with this body. Never mind that. Why don't you pick up, no matter how many times I call? Did you divert my calls somewhere you shouldn't have?
